meta.description: Research ocean D&D and ship costs

user.t:
Web research (read-only; no installs; no files except your answer). Date-stamp 2026-10-11. Context: scoup.ai recovers truck detention and audits freight invoices with a deterministic clock/free-time/rate engine and evidence packets. The founder asked whether we can make "renting cargo ships cheaper" and cut other time-varying costs. Research with cited real sources (grade A/B/C):
1. Ocean container demurrage & detention (D&D) for importers/exporters: the US FMC final rule on D&D billing practices (46 CFR part 541, OSRA 2022) — effective date, required invoice elements, deadline to issue invoices (30 days?), consequences when a carrier/terminal fails the requirements (charge not payable?), dispute window and response duties, who may be billed. Also FMC 46 CFR 545.5 incentive principle. FMC enforcement/refund statistics, charge refunds via the FMC Charge Complaint process, and estimates of total D&D charged (FMC D&D data collection, Container Xchange/other reports). Typical free time and per-diem tariffs (public D&D tariffs of Maersk, MSC, CMA CGM, Hapag-Lloyd for a US port; escalating daily rates). EU/UK equivalents if any.
2. Is D&D audit a fit for an engine like ours (clock start/stop events from carrier/terminal milestones, free days, tiered per-day rates, invoice-content compliance check)? Which public data feeds give the needed timestamps (carrier track & trace APIs, DCSA standards, terminal availability), and who already sells D&D audit (e.g. Expedock, Kpler? Portcast, Vizion, Cargoes Flow, Shipwell, ODeX) with prices.
3. Ship chartering ("renting cargo ships"): who charters (bulk shippers, traders) vs who our customers are; public price data (Baltic Dry Index, Harpex/Howe Robinson container charter index, Clarksons, Drewry WCI, Freightos FBX, SCFI) — which have free historical downloads with direct URLs and licences; whether forecasting charter rates is credible (academic evidence on BDI/freight rate forecastability vs random walk; cite papers).
4. Recommend: should scoup pursue ocean D&D audit and/or charter-rate features? Size the pain per importer (e.g. D&D $ per container, containers per mid-size importer) with sources.
Return a compact report (~1200 words, tables, URL + grade for every number), flag weak evidence.

handback.t:
## Ocean D&D and charter-rate research for scoup.ai (date-stamp 2026-10-11)

Grades: **A** = primary source (statute or regulator text, or the carrier's or index publisher's own page). **B** = reputable trade press or law firm. **C** = blog, startup site, unverified, or my own inference. I read every A source directly unless a note says otherwise.

### 1. US ocean D&D rules (46 CFR part 541, OSRA 2022)

| Item | Finding | Source / grade |
|---|---|---|
| Final rule | Issued 2024-02-26; effective 2024-05-28. The invoice-contents section (§541.6) also took effect 2024-05-28, after OMB approved it on 2024-04-16 | https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2024/05/update-on-fmcs-final-rule-on-demurrage-and-detention-billing-practices (B); https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2024-10515.pdf (A, not opened) |
| Who may be billed (§541.4) | Only (a) the party that contracted for the ocean transport or storage, or (b) the consignee, meaning the ultimate recipient of the cargo. Never several parties at once | autocare.org summary of the rule (B) |
| Required invoice contents (§541.6) | B/L number; container number(s); port of discharge; basis of liability; invoice date and due date; free time allowed with its start and end dates; container availability date (import) or earliest return date (export); the specific dates charged; the rule applied (tariff or contract number); the rate(s); total due; a contact; a URL or QR code for disputes; dispute timeframes; and a certification that the charges comply and that the biller's own performance did not cause them | https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/46/541.6 (A) |
| Missing element | "Failure to include any of the required minimum information … eliminates any obligation of the billed party to pay" | https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/46/541.5 (A) |
| 30-day deadline (§541.7) | The invoice must be issued within 30 calendar days of the date the charge was last incurred. If it is late, "the billed party is not required to pay the charge". An NVOCC has 30 days from the invoice it received | https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/46/541.7 (A) |
| Disputes (§541.8) | The billed party gets at least 30 days from issue to ask for mitigation, refund or waiver. The billing party must try to resolve it within 30 days unless both agree to longer | https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/46/541.8 (A) |
| Incentive principle (46 CFR 545.5) | D&D is reasonable only if it gives an incentive for freight to move. Charging when cargo is not available, or detention when an empty cannot be returned, is "likely to be found unreasonable". The FMC also looks at notice and at government inspection holds | https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/46/545.5 (A) |

**Enforcement**
- **Hapag-Lloyd invoices (open case):** the FMC opened an investigation (Docket CC-002) into 159 Hapag-Lloyd invoices worth $1,191,470 that were re-issued more than 30 days late. It came from an NVOCC charge complaint filed in February 2025. https://dpiusa.com/signals/signals-headlines-march-6-2026/ (B)
- **MSC:** fined $22.67M on 2026-01-06. About $13.1M of that was for D&D overcharging on non-operating reefers in 2021, and $65k for billing customs brokers as notify parties. https://chaloslaw.com/fmc-hits-msc-with-civil-penalty-of-22-67-million/ (B)
- **Maersk:** $1.9M penalty for bi
[...]
hapag-lloyd.[REDACTED:high_entropy].pdf (A, but the PDF would not parse, so this is from a snippet: B) |

**EU and UK:** I found no binding equivalent to the FMC rule. The only thing I found is soft law, the FIATA best-practices guide, which the European Shippers' Council endorses (container-news.com/fiata-detention-demurrage-charges, C). The EU consortia block exemption lapsed in 2024; that is from memory and unverified. **Weak evidence.**

### 2. Does D&D audit fit our engine?

**Yes, it fits closely.** It is the same pattern as truck detention: a clock start event, a clock stop event, free days that can be working days or calendar days, tiered day rates, and a check of the invoice against a required element list. Part 541 goes further than anything in trucking: it makes a missing element, or an invoice issued after 30 days, legally not payable. That makes it a deterministic rule, a good match for an evidence packet. Three things make it harder than truck detention:
- holidays and working-day calendars per terminal;
- terminal closures and availability (for example, CMA CGM does not charge demurrage when the terminal is closed);
- separate charges from carriers and from terminal operators.

**Where the timestamps come from**
- **DCSA Track & Trace (3.0):** standard equipment events. GTOT is the full container gating out of the destination terminal, which starts detention. GTIN with an empty container is the empty return, which stops it. https://developer.dcsa.org/explore-apis/track-and-trace (A)
- **Aggregators:** Vizion (Core plan from $119/month; the professional tier adds terminal events, price on request). https://vizionapi.com/container-tracking/pricing (A)
- **Terminal49:** last free day, holds and fees for US terminals ("for most terminals but not all"). It meters per container but publishes no dollar rates. https://terminal49.com/api-pricing (A)

**Who already sells D&D audit**

None of these publish prices:
- **Visibility tools:** Terminal49, GoComet, Beacon (beacon.com/solutions/demurrage-and-detention-final), BuyCo (buyco.co).
- **Freight-audit firms:** Intelligent Audit, which has a D&D invoice-validation case study (intelligentaudit.com), and nVision Global.
- **Early-stage:** FreeTimeLedger (g2.com/sellers/freetimeledger), which tests charges against Part 541. Grade C.

I found no evidence that Expedock, Kpler, Portcast or Shipwell sell D&D audit specifically. Their prices are unknown.

### 3. Chartering ships ("renting cargo ships")

**Who charters:** container lines charter ships from tonnage owners, and commodity traders and miners charter bulk carriers. Our customers (shippers, forwarders, 3PLs) buy space per container. They never charter a ship. That is my inference from the structure of the industry, so grade C, but well established.

**Index data and licences**

| Index | Access | Source / grade |
|---|---|---|
| Baltic Dry Index (BDI) | Paid licence. Redistribution without one breaches Baltic Exchange terms | https://www.balticexchange.com/en/site-services/data-policy.html (A) |
| HARPEX (container charter) | Latest 2,468 on 09-Oct-2026. "The full HARPEX Series is available by subscription" | https://www.harperpetersen.com/harpex (A) |
| Drewry WCI | $4,351 per 40 ft on 2026-10-08. Free with registration; all rights reserved | https://www.drewry.co.uk/supply-chain-advisors/supply-chain-expertise/world-container-index-assessed-by-drewry (A) |
| Freightos FBX | History from 2016, licensed through the Baltic Exchange | https://www.balticexchange.com/en/data-services/market-information0/container-services.html (A) |
| SCFI | Free to view weekly; terms not verified | Shanghai Shipping Exchange (C) |
| Clarksons | Paid | Not checked |

**None of these has a clearly licensed free historical download.**

**Can charter rates be forecast?** There is no consensus that models beat simple benchmarks:
- An NTNU thesis found that multivariate one-month forecasts could not beat a univariate seasonal model out of sample. https://core.ac.uk/works/123639579 (C, thesis)
- Kjeldsberg, Munim & Schramm (2026, *Maritime Economics & Logistics*) reviewed 28 machine-learning studies. "Hybrid" models often beat standalone ones, no architecture is reliably best, and 61% of the studies are on dry bulk. https://research.cbs.dk/en/publications/machine-learning-in-freight-rate-forecasting-a-systematic-literat/ (A)
- Batchelor, Alizadeh & Visvikis (2007), *International Journal of Forecasting* 23(1):101–114 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/intfor/v23y2007i1p101-114.html) is the standard reference, but I could not read the abstract, so its findings are unverified (C).
- **Weak evidence overall.** Under our honesty rule (no unmeasured claims), a charter forecasting feature cannot be claimed as accurate.

### 4. Recommendation and pain sizing

- **Do pursue an ocean D&D invoice-compliance audit for US imports.** Start with the deterministic Part 541 checks: missing elements, the 30-day deadline, wrong billed party, and free time and tier arithmetic. Then add §545.5 checks on availability and empty returns, using DCSA, Terminal49 or Vizion timestamps.
- **Do not build charter or rate forecasting.** It does not fit our customers, the data needs paid licences, and forecasting skill is unproven.

**Pain sizing (rough):**
- $15.4B over 5 years is about **$3.1B a year** across 9 carriers (FMC, A).
- US containerized imports were 25.66M TEU in 2024 (JOC via search snippet, B). That gives roughly **$120 per import TEU** (my calculation, C). It overstates because exports are in the total, and understates because terminal charges and other carriers are excluded.
- A container held two weeks cost about $2,700 at LA/LB in 2022. That was the peak year. https://maritime-executive.com/article/report-american-ports-top-the-list-for-d-d-fees-worldwide (B)
- At today's tariffs, 10 days past free time costs about $2,300–2,900 per box (Maersk tiers).
- **Illustration only:** a mid-size importer at 2,000 TEU a year would have about $240k a year of D&D exposure. The 2,000 TEU figure is my assumption; I found no source for how many containers a mid-size importer moves. I also found no evidence for the share of D&D invoices that are non-compliant. The Hapag case, about $7.5k per invoice, is one example.
- The figure of "1.1–2.3M D&D invoices a year" circulates citing FMC estimates, but I could not trace it to an FMC document (C).

**Biggest gaps:** containers per importer, the error and recovery rate on D&D invoices, competitors' prices, and EU/UK rules. All need primary validation, ideally invoice samples from pilot customers.

No files were created or changed in the repository.
